claims.text: Controlled annealing followed by quenching can control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Controlled thermal treatment promotes the formation of desired constituent phases.
As-cast or as-solidified Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs have a largely homogeneous phase structure.
The initial phase structure is disordered.
Annealing in the 600–800°C range followed by rapid quenching is an applicable treatment for this alloy system.
The treatment should be conducted under an inert atmosphere with controlled temperature profiles, holding times, and cooling rates.
The thermal treatment causes grain-boundary rearrangements.
Atomic diffusion during treatment drives phase segregation.
Annealing increases atomic mobility by supplying thermal energy.
Increased atomic mobility fosters phase separation.
Increased atomic mobility fosters nucleation of more stable phases.
Rapid quenching freezes the annealed microstructure into a state with a refined phase distribution.
The treated alloy will have a more controlled and refined distribution of constituent phases than the as-cast alloy.
The treatment may improve the consistency of mechanical properties.
Untreated as-cast samples have broader and less controlled phase distributions.
Composition variation beyond a narrow tolerance may limit the effectiveness of thermal treatment.
Failure to precisely control annealing and quenching parameters may limit treatment effectiveness.
The optimal annealing temperature, holding time, and phase-transformation kinetics remain uncertain without direct experimental validation.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as largely homogeneous, while the baseline is described as having a broader and less controlled phase distribution; without clarification of whether these refer to spatial homogeneity, disorder, or the number and fractions of phases, the descriptions are in tension.
